name: Vistra
headline: A large US power generator with a Texas retail electricity business that hedges with its own plants.
what_short: Power generation and retail electricity, US
what_it_does: Vistra sells electricity into wholesale power markets from 43,641 MW of plants (gas 62%, coal 20%, nuclear 15%, solar and batteries 3%). It also sells electricity to households and businesses, notably in Texas, where customers can switch suppliers. Its retail arm buys power at market prices.
why_it_passed: Its retail business, the part that decides the verdict, has sold electricity in Texas's competitive market for over 20 years and keeps its customers through service and integrated supply.
Owning its own generation hedges the retail book against power price swings.
Retail customer counts rose by about 3%, 3% and 1% a year in 2020 to 2022 by meters.
A federal nuclear production tax credit runs from 2024 to 2032, which supports the cash from its nuclear plants.
why_not_now: At $141.73 a share the cash the business produces is only about 2.2% of the price, compared with 5.31% on a 30-year US Treasury bond. The analysis counts only the case with no growth, worth $26.02 a share, so the price is more than five times that value.
watch: Total debt is about $20.7 billion, and S&P rates it BBB-, the lowest investment-grade rating; $1.5 billion of junior notes were added in September 2026.
In Winter Storm Uri in 2021, one weather event produced a large loss across its Texas generation, and collateral demands can drain cash quickly.
It has bought back shares with borrowed money at prices far above the value range.
no_fair_reason: After subtracting its large debt, the cash the business produces does not earn the required return at any positive price on the analysis's main basis, so its fair price comes out below zero.
